clinicalPearls: Results from failure of the embryonic hyaloid vascular system and primary vitreous to regress, usually unilateral and in an otherwise healthy full-term infant
Typically presents with leukocoria, microphthalmia and, in the anterior form, a retrolental fibrovascular membrane with elongated ciliary processes drawn centrally
Anterior disease can produce a shallow anterior chamber, cataract and secondary angle-closure glaucoma; posterior disease features a vitreous stalk and retinal folds or dysplasia
A persistent Bergmeister papilla or Mittendorf dot may be seen as mild residua of the hyaloid system
The critical differential is retinoblastoma, and any child with leukocoria requires urgent specialist assessment
Ultrasound and MRI help distinguish the fibrovascular stalk and absence of calcification from a calcified retinoblastoma
Early vitreoretinal surgery may preserve the eye and, in selected anterior cases, some vision, but the visual prognosis is generally guarded
reference.pathophysiology: During normal development the hyaloid artery and primary vitreous nourish the developing lens and regress before birth. In persistent fetal vasculature this regression fails, leaving hyperplastic fibrovascular tissue in the vitreous cavity and behind the lens. The retained tissue exerts traction, causing microphthalmia, a retrolental membrane with dragged ciliary processes, cataract and, posteriorly, a vitreous stalk with retinal folds or dysplasia. Contraction and neovascular activity can precipitate cataract, shallowing of the anterior chamber, secondary glaucoma and vitreous haemorrhage. Most cases are sporadic and unilateral, though bilateral disease raises suspicion of a systemic or genetic disorder.
additionalInvestigations: B-scan ocular ultrasound to define the fibrovascular stalk and detect calcification
MRI of the orbits and brain when retinoblastoma cannot be excluded clinically
Examination under anaesthesia with fundus assessment of both eyes
Intraocular pressure measurement and biometry for microphthalmia
Consideration of genetic evaluation in bilateral or syndromic presentations
redFlags: Leukocoria that could represent retinoblastoma requiring urgent exclusion
Bilateral disease suggesting Norrie disease or a systemic disorder
Secondary angle-closure glaucoma threatening a painful blind eye
Rapid progression of cataract or vitreous haemorrhage
Signs of raised intraocular pressure or buphthalmos
reference.prognosis: Visual outcome is usually poor, particularly in posterior or combined disease, though early surgery for selected anterior cases can salvage the eye and occasionally yield useful vision; the priority is often preserving a comfortable, cosmetically acceptable globe.
pitfalls: Attributing leukocoria to PHPV without excluding retinoblastoma
Failing to examine the fellow eye and consider a bilateral systemic cause
Missing evolving secondary glaucoma in a microphthalmic eye
Delaying referral and losing the window for sight-preserving surgery
references: Taylor & Hoyt's Paediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
management: Urgently exclude retinoblastoma before any intervention in a child with leukocoria
Early lensectomy, vitrectomy and excision of the retrolental fibrovascular membrane for selected, predominantly anterior disease
Aggressive amblyopia therapy with optical correction and occlusion of the fellow eye, which is central to any visual gain
Detect and control secondary glaucoma medically or surgically with intraocular pressure monitoring
Aim to preserve a comfortable, cosmetically acceptable globe when useful vision is not achievable
Genetic and systemic evaluation in bilateral or syndromic presentations
Long-term paediatric ophthalmology follow-up through a specialist team
